brief.head: Keep the yolk
brief.text: Dietary cholesterol has nothing to do with the cholesterol in our body, Amit Varma said, calling the egg yolk perhaps the healthiest food known to man. {009-C07}

brief.head: Salad, then dessert
brief.text: Eating order matters, Amit Varma found: fibre first, protein second, carbs last. The Western meal of salad, main course and dessert turns out to be ideal. {009-C10}

brief.text: Multivitamins are “kinda like a five-star buffet”, said Amit Varma, passing on his nutritionist friend Shruti Jahagirdar’s advice. Work out what you lack and take that instead. {009-C20}

brief.head: Remember the Emergency
brief.text: Recommending Coomi Kapoor’s *The Emergency*, Amit Varma argued it was no aberration: India’s constitution centralised power, and a dominant state is in the Indian state’s DNA. {009-C22}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma on how he reversed his type 2 diabetes
lead.head: Reversed, one meal a day
body: Amit Varma’s doctor prescribed metformin and the usual drugs. When Varma asked about diet, the doctor looked embarrassed and said only: “You’re a smart man, you know what to do.” {009-S08}
Varma sensed, he said, that the doctor knew everything he had been taught was wrong but could not say so.
In fact Varma did know. He had read the books and gifted Jason Fung’s *The Diabetes Code* to friends. “Intellectually I knew, but I was too lazy,” he said.

What closed the gap was a sensor on the arm. His co-host Ajay Shah suggested a continuous glucose monitor, or CGM, and Varma watched in real time what each meal did to his blood. Guided by it, he moved to keto and then to one meal a day, and his HbA1c fell from 7.7 to 5.7.
“It is reversible, type 2 diabetes, it can be reversed through diet alone,” Varma said. “It is a disease of the diet.” {009-C05}
Any doctor who says otherwise, he added, is “a lying quack”.
## A hormone, not a helping

The episode’s backbone was Gary Taubes’s *The Case Against Sugar*. Taubes argues that sugars cause diabetes and obesity in the same sense that cigarettes cause lung cancer: through their hormonal effects, not because we eat too much. {009-C01}
Sugar, Varma said, hits the brain’s reward centre like nicotine or alcohol, yet we never feel withdrawal, because we are never without it for long.
Every meal brings an insulin spike, and frequent spikes push the body towards insulin resistance. So small frequent meals, a dietitian’s staple, “are terrible”, he said.
## How the dogma set
Why were we told otherwise? Varma traced a century of error, from a physician who blamed the motor car to a sugar lobby that Franklin Roosevelt could not beat.

The turning point was Ancel Keys, whose Seven Countries Study blamed saturated fat for heart disease. Keys, Varma said, cherry-picked his countries, and by 1961 the American Heart Association was urging low-fat diets. {009-S04}
Varma called what the sugar lobby did “a far greater scandal” than anything the tobacco lobby did.
He did not spare the people behind it. When he thinks of Keys or the prominent people in the sugar lobby, he said, “I think of them as men who committed crimes on humanity.”
## Know thyself

Shah, who has worn a CGM for his own experiments, reframed the lesson. We are usually handed a diet, he said, when we should start from our own tastes and food culture and adapt them to our bodies. {009-C08}

His findings were precise. Sugar behaves differently alone, with fat and with spices. White rice and maida are “merely polymerised sugars”. And a calorie is not a calorie: complex carbs feed the microbes in the gut, which eat some of the energy.
Varma urged scepticism of nutrition studies, whose funders deserve scrutiny while the sugar lobby remains powerful.
Varma did not want to sell anyone a diet. “Why should you listen to me?” he asked. Read the books, he said, get a CGM and figure out what works for you.
His closing advice came in two parts: “One, know thyself and two, sugar is poison.”

second.label: The fat theory
second.head: Keys to a bad diet
second.deck: How one study’s choice of countries turned America against fat
body: In the late 1950s Ancel Keys published his Seven Countries Study, which appeared to link saturated fat with heart disease.

Amit Varma called it “deeply intellectually dishonest”. To test a hypothesis, he said, you must examine whatever could disprove it. Keys left out France, with its high-fat diet and low heart disease, as well as Switzerland and Germany. His chosen countries also ate a lot of sugar, which he skipped over. {009-S04}

The American Heart Association argued against him in 1957. By 1960 he sat on its main panel, and in 1961 it issued low-fat guidelines. Obesity, Varma said, went from about one in seven Americans to one in three over the next forty years. {#obesity}

quote.text: He cherry picks the countries, then he cherry picks the evidence, then he comes to the conclusion that fat is the problem.

third.head: How sugar lit a Camel
body: Until 1913, cigarette smoke was alkaline, Amit Varma said, so anyone who tried to inhale it would start coughing. {009-S02}
That year a new brand, Camel, arrived. Its makers raised the carbohydrate content of the tobacco, and so its sugar. The smoke turned acidic, became easy to inhale, and became more addictive.

“I would say that in a sense, sugars enabled smoking to cause lung cancer,” Varma said. He had the history from Gary Taubes’s *The Case Against Sugar*, which he called the best overarching look at the subject. {009-R01}

Varma found sugar’s pull summed up in Michael Pollan’s *The Botany of Desire*. Pollan describes his son Isaac’s first taste of birthday-cake icing and imagines him exclaiming: “Your world contains this. From this day onwards I shall dedicate my life to it.” {009-J10}
third.caption: the sweetened Camel

p2.title: Sugar on trial
p2.deck: How sugar escaped blame for a century, and what a sensor on the arm reveals

sections.label: The charge
sections.head: Worse than a sweet tooth
sections.caption: sugar’s hormonal harm
body: Amit Varma began with a reading list: Sidney Mintz’s *Sweetness and Power*, Nina Teicholz’s *The Big Fat Surprise*, and Jason Fung’s *The Obesity Code* and *The Diabetes Code*. {009-R05}

But the key book, he said, was Gary Taubes’s *The Case Against Sugar*. Michael Pollan once called Taubes “a Solzhenitsyn of the nutrition world”, for taking on dogmas from the late 1990s on. {009-J09}

Taubes argues that sugars such as sucrose and high-fructose corn syrup cause diabetes and obesity in the same sense that smoking causes lung cancer, “not because we eat too much of these sugars”, but through their hormonal effects. {009-C01}
## A slow-acting poison
They are not short-term toxins, Taubes writes, but do their damage over years and decades, perhaps even from generation to generation, through what mothers eat and how that changes the womb.

Varma calls sugar the most addictive substance out there. It acts on the brain’s reward centre as nicotine and alcohol do. Too much coffee leaves you jittery; sugar gives no such warning. And since we are never without it, we never feel withdrawal. {009-C02}
~ The charge sheet runs on. Varma linked sugar to hypertension and heart disease, said researchers are studying its links with cancer, and noted that some call Alzheimer’s disease “type 3 diabetes”.

quote.text: We will never experience a withdrawal symptom because we are never without sugar for long enough to experience that withdrawal symptom.

sections.label: The history
sections.head: Blame it on the motor car
sections.caption: the motor car and other suspects
body: In 1907 Kailas Chunder Bose, “a fellow Bengali” of Amit Varma’s, observed that with prosperity under British rule, “the number of diabetic cases has enormously increased.” {009-J11}

Early physicians linked diabetes to carbohydrates. But Elliott Joslin, who became America’s most prominent diabetes physician, looked elsewhere. In 1925 he said automobiles cause diabetes: people stopped walking, got fat, then got diabetes.
His ally Harold Himsworth wrote a paper, now known to be flawed, blaming fat. Meanwhile Prohibition pushed Americans from alcohol to candy, and sugar consumption soared.

Nobody joined the dots, Varma said. Physicians understood hormones but not diet; nutritionists lacked the medical insight. So other theories took root, “then cabals build along those theories, careers are based on those theories”. {009-S03}
## Wealth, or culture?
Ajay Shah asked whether all this was simply income elasticity. Partly, Varma said, but Japan, France and Germany grew prosperous without the same result. Culture mattered too.

He recalled the Dalit scholar Chandra Bhan Prasad, whose obese, diabetic village elders fill him with pride: a couple of generations ago, they would not have been prosperous enough to get diabetes. {009-S06}
~ Prasad says much the same of the ghunghat. Lower-caste women were not allowed to wear it, so a Dalit bride who wears one is exercising a choice she was once denied.

quote.text: When I go back to my village and I see my village elders are obese and they have diabetes, my heart fills with pride.
quote.who: Chandra Bhan Prasad, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: The lobby
sections.head: Fat framed, sugar walks
sections.caption: the sugar lobby
body: By the 1930s, Amit Varma said, two dogmas were forming: that fat causes chronic diseases such as heart disease, and that obesity is simply calories in exceeding calories out.

The sugar lobby, meanwhile, grew mighty. Franklin Roosevelt called it the most powerful interest group he had seen. “This is a man who won World War II in a sense,” Varma said, “but couldn’t beat the sugar lobby.” {009-J13}

Critics were brutally shut down. In 1976 Jean Mayer wrote a *New York Times* piece about the bitter truth of sugar. *Reader’s Digest* planned to run excerpts until calls were made to its managing editor, and it was spiked. {009-S05}
In 1977 the US Senate’s dietary goals recommended a low-fat diet and said sugar was perfectly fine. On a chart from Nina Teicholz’s book, Varma said, American obesity shoots up from around then.
## Why the myth survives

The pushback continues from three sources, he said: corporate interests hiding sugar behind labels such as “no added sugar”; Paul Graham’s “aggressively conventional minded”; and self-interested defenders of the status quo, including doctors trained the wrong way. {009-C04}
~ In India, he warned, going to a doctor over forty is dangerous unless they have kept updating themselves. If you graduated in 2010 or even a little later, “chances are you’re wrong.”

quote.text: It’s hard to imagine now the heat of the passion. It was just like we had desecrated the American flag.
quote.who: David Kritchevsky, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The sensor
sections.head: Your blood, in real time
sections.caption: his time in range
body: Ajay Shah, who had suggested the CGM to Amit Varma, put the lesson his own way. We are usually handed a diet, he said; we should instead start from our own tastes and food culture, and adapt them until they work for our bodies. {009-C08}

HbA1c, he said, is a smeared average of three months of blood sugar. A CGM shows the picture moment by moment, so surges and volatility become visible. His rule of thumb is to stay between 70 and 160 for over 80 per cent of the day, and never below 70. {009-C09}
## What sugar keeps company with

Shah tested one dose of sugar alone, with fat, and with fat plus spices such as ginger, nutmeg and cinnamon. Each produced a different surge. If you must have sugar, he said, make it ice cream, ideally spiced. {009-C11}
Simple starches are no refuge. A hundred grams of white rice, he said, is “pretty much the same” as a hundred grams of sugar, one reaction with the enzyme amylase away. {009-C12}
A CGM is expensive, but habits form in two or three months, so Shah suggested two or three rigorous months on one each year. {009-C13}
~ Food is social, he added. If there is cheesecake in the fridge it will end up inside you, so change what the household buys, even if that means being “rude”.

quote.text: We should try to stay between 70 and 160 for over 80 percent of the day.

sections.label: The gut
sections.head: The microbes take their cut
sections.caption: the gut microbiome
body: Calorie counts come from burning food in pure oxygen, Ajay Shah said, and that may not be how the body processes it.
He began with plants. In hydroponics, plants fed simple chemical fertiliser underinvest in their root microbiome, and lose nutritional quality and the ability to fight disease. {009-C16}
Simple carbs, he said, do the same to us. They are absorbed soon after the stomach, so the gut microbiome is not fed and shrivels. Complex carbs travel all the way down and feed it.

A paper by Corbin and colleagues in *Nature Communications* in June 2023 compared diets with identical calories. On some measures the gut microbiome was 8x higher on complex carbs, and the microbes ate some of the energy: a difference of about 200 calories a day. {009-C15}
## Read the label, and the study
Labels mislead, Amit Varma warned. Shah named one standard trick, concentrated apple juice: “a way of getting sugar in and saying this is hundred percent fruit”.
Varma urged readers to check who funded a nutrition study and how it was done, and to trust meta-studies over single ones. {009-C19}
~ Told that a glass of wine is good for the heart, Varma asked what it does to the liver. Shah added that studies show the best amount of alcohol is zero.

quote.text: Look at each study with a default position of being critical of it and then figuring out what’s going on there.

side.boxText: Gary Taubes, an award-winning science journalist, argues that sugar causes diabetes and obesity the way smoking causes lung cancer. Amit Varma called *The Case Against Sugar* the best overarching look at the subject, and for him the most definitive. {009-R01}

contQuote.text: In the world of diet, we are normally told, here’s a diet. Whereas what we should be asking is where are my preferences? And what are my tastes and what is my food culture?

p3.deck: Poker, a mountain, a chess rating and a boss who made people cry

stories.start: So when I discovered all of this about five, six years ago
stories.end: and my HBA1C went from 7.7 to 5.7. I'd reversed type 2 diabetes
stories.caption: reversing his own diabetes
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how he gained, lost and regained the weight
stories.head: Dealt a bad hand at 107 kg
body: Amit Varma spent five years as a professional poker player. It paid better than anything else he could have done, he said, but it was corrosive as a lifestyle: “You play a 15-hour session, go home and sleep, play another 15-hour session.” {#poker}

About five or six years before the episode, when he discovered the books, he weighed 105 kg. He read them, took up keto with intermittent fasting, ran every day, and lost about 20 kg. At 85 or 86 kg he was full of energy, even ran a 10k, and held that weight for a long time.
Then COVID made him sedentary. Whenever he needed comfort, it was biryani or pizza. “It’s just one meal,” he said. “And so one meal at a time, I went in the wrong direction, went to 107.” {009-S07}
About 18 months before the episode he was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, with an HbA1c of 7.7. Three months on metformin changed little.
Then Ajay Shah suggested a continuous glucose monitor. Varma wore one through three two-week cycles. A slice of toast sent his glucose to 285; eggs and bacon left a flat line.

He moved to keto and intermittent fasting, then to one meal a day, eaten between six and eight after cooking two- or three-course dinners to music. He calls it a really happy period. His HbA1c fell from 7.7 to 5.7. {#hba1c}
~ He is now at around 95 kg, no longer on keto, and plans to reach 85 before settling into intermittent fasting with low carbs.
stories.why: Knowing is not doing. Varma had gifted *The Diabetes Code* to friends while staying too lazy to act. Seeing his own body’s response closed the gap, and convinced him type 2 diabetes is “a disease of the diet”. {009-C05}
stories.postscript: A friend who swore by oats tried a CGM: oats took her to 280, eggs flatlined, and she lost 25 kg. {009-S09}

stories.start: I want to tell a little story that uh last month
stories.end: when we take the meal, we get a complex smear of these things
stories.caption: the three surges
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s CGM, on a hike near Dharamshala
stories.head: A summit meal in three acts
body: A month or two before the episode, Ajay Shah was hiking in the hills near Dharamshala, wearing a CGM. At the top he had a 500 ml bottle of Gatorade, white rice and rajma.
Then he walked continuously downhill for 1,000 metres. {#descend} Eaten on the plains, he said, such a meal would bring an indistinct mess of a surge, elevated for hours.

Burning energy fast, he instead saw “three distinct surges”, each burned off in turn: first the Gatorade’s sugar, then the white rice as amylase turned it into sugar, and last the rajma’s complex carbs. {009-S10}
~ “I vividly saw what they tell us in the books,” Shah said: simple sugar reaches the blood immediately, while complex carbs take their time.
stories.why: Everyday life smears overlapping signals together and hides cause and effect. On an empty stomach and a steep descent, the textbook timing of sugar, starch and complex carbs became visible. Shah stressed that he does not recommend the meal.
stories.postscript: Amit Varma admitted the story made him crave rajma, “despite the windy things it does to you the next morning”.

stories.start: one of the side effects of sugar that I didn't mention
stories.end: or even more if I add a biryani to the pizza
stories.caption: his chess rating
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on sugar, brain fog and bullet chess
stories.head: A pizza costs 150 points
body: One side effect of sugar that Amit Varma had not yet mentioned is brain fog. Off keto, he said, he tires sooner and thinks far worse. {#fog}

He has an objective measure. He plays bullet chess on chess.com, a whole bunch of games every day, under a pseudonym: “no one shall ever know.” He plays as an addict, not to improve, so his rating holds steady.
On keto, it climbs about 150 points. After a cheat day with pizza, it drops about 150, “or even more if I add a biryani to the pizza”. {009-S11}
~ Pizza plus biryani, Varma said, is a little like Louis CK’s “bang bang”: one complete meal in one restaurant, then straight into another with a different cuisine for another complete meal.
stories.why: Sugar’s cost to clear thinking is real, and it can be measured. Any activity done consistently every day can serve as a personal gauge of how well the mind is working.

stories.start: I gotta tell you that uh yesterday I was hanging with uh
stories.end: And all the good stuff in the world happens like that
stories.caption: the boss who made people cry
stories.kicker: A former colleague’s verdict on Ajay Shah
stories.head: The monster they returned to
body: The day before recording, Amit Varma met a former colleague of Ajay Shah’s, who spent four years with him at the finance ministry and many years at the UN.
Shah, she said, was horrible to work with, “a monster”. “He would make me cry,” she said, and it happened to everyone. “But we always used to come back and work with him again.” {009-S01}

Why? Because they learnt so much, she said, and learnt how to learn. Put to Shah, the charge drew an economist’s answer: “The most interesting stuff in life is just the invisible spillovers that are not intermediated by the market system.” {009-C18}

~ We are each a linear combination of our influences, Shah said, and impose externalities on one another, sometimes positive, sometimes negative. All the good stuff in the world, he added, happens like that.
stories.why: Demanding mentors hurt at the time and transform people later. Shah calls such influence an externality: unpriced, invisible, and in his view the place where most of the good in the world happens.
stories.postscript: Varma’s reply: “I keep telling my writing students, don’t use jargon, don’t use jargon. Look what you just did.” {009-J02}

quiz.q: What did Camel’s makers change in 1913, and why did that matter to smokers?
quiz.a: They raised the sugar content, so the smoke turned acidic, inhalable and more addictive.

quiz.q: Which high-fat, low-heart-disease country did Ancel Keys leave out of his famous study?
quiz.a: France, along with Switzerland and Germany, which could have disproved his hypothesis.

quiz.q: What happened when Amit Varma’s oat-loving friend finally wore a CGM?
quiz.a: Oats sent her glucose to 280, eggs flatlined, and she lost 25 kg.

quiz.q: Within what band does Ajay Shah aim to keep his blood sugar, and how often?
quiz.a: Between 70 and 160, for over 80 per cent of the day.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, do complex carbs earn a calorie discount?
quiz.a: They reach the gut microbiome, and the microbes eat some of the energy.

quiz.q: What does Amit Varma use as an objective measure of his brain fog?
quiz.a: His bullet-chess rating, which climbs about 150 points on keto and falls after pizza.
